The future tense (an aimsir fháistineach) is one of the most important tenses for your oral Irish exam. You will use it to talk about your plans, your ambitions, and what life will look like after school.

threads.title: An aimsir fháistineach - homework
threads.body:
Hi everyone 

I’m wondering is it correct that ‘ I will get’ is different than ‘ I will get up’ 

So it changes from Gheobhaidh mé to Eireoidh mé

This isn’t the first time I’ve noticed the verb change to another depending what function is after and it’s confusing me terribly. 
I try to do the homework using the notes but I find myself having to translate to make sure I understand what’s right/wrong. 

Thank you

comments.body: I am just doing the homework Jennifer and was confused with this one too, thanks for asking the question. I dont have the answer but hopefully someone will😊

Gheobhaidh mé - Is to get a thing
Eireoidh mé - Means to arise 

So, to get up in Irish is actually "I arise in the morning." 
As far as I know anyway - The way I personally think about how to differentiate is the actual function. You wouldnt get "up" like you would get a "present". You would not recieve the idea of "Up" as a physical thing.

Hey guys, yes Geoffrey explained it well there. In english when we say 'to get up from bed' but it is a more colloquial saying that everyone uses! But in Irish the verb we use is 'Éirigh' as in 'arise'. This is then different from the very 'To get'. 'To get' is the irregular verb 'faigh' which is written as 'Gheobhaidh mé/tú/...' in the future tense.

threads.title: Prepositions
threads.body: Hi guys, just wondering with the prepositions is there a way to know which to use/when they're needed, or do we need to just learn them off? I'm not sure if that makes sense just struggling to grasp them, thanks!

comments.body:
Hey Jade,

Great question, and it makes perfect sense. The honest answer is that there is no rule that tells you which preposition goes with which verb, so you learn them as a pair, not separately. The trick is that you never learn "ar" on its own, you learn the whole chunk.

A few you will use constantly:

- éisteacht le: éistim le ceol (I listen to music)
- cur suas le: cuirim suas le mo dheartháir (I put up with my brother)
- bheith ag caint le: bhí mé ag caint le mo chara (I was talking with my friend)
- cabhrú le: chabhraigh mé le mo mháthair (I helped my mother) 
- ag smaoineamh ar: bím ag smaoineamh ar an scrúdú (I think about the exam)

Start a page in your copy with two columns, the verb and its preposition, and add one or two a week from whatever topic you are working on. Do not try to learn a list of forty. Little and often here beats a big session, because you will meet the same ten or so over and over in the oral.

Say them out loud in a full sentence about yourself. That is what makes them stick, not staring at the list.

If you write out five sentences using them, fire them over to me here and I'll take a look 🙂
Go raibh maith agat!😊

threads.title: An aimsir chaite question
threads.body: dia duit, i was going through some of the verbs conjugating them in an aimsir chaite and i can across the verb éirigh (to get up), i was wondering why when conjugating this verb for the 'we' it's d'éiríomar instead of d'eirigheamar. Is this because it's easier to say or is there another reason that I should be aware of?

comments.body: You use the root of the verb - éir  -  remove "igh". If you look back on Monday nights class Eamon goes through this or you can just use muid instead when speaking. Hope this helps

Hey Aisling,

good question, and Jenna is right on the root.

Éirigh is a second conjugation verb (the -igh ones like ceannaigh, imigh, cabhraigh). With those, you drop the -igh and add the ending, so éir + íomar gives d'éiríomar. The d' goes on because the verb starts with a vowel.

So:
d'éirigh mé
d'éirigh tú
d'éirigh sé/sí
d'éiríomar (or d'éirigh muid)
d'éirigh sibh
d'éirigh siad

Compare it with a first conjugation verb like ól: d'ólamar, where the ending goes straight onto the root.

The spelling you were expecting is the older pre-standard one, so you will see it in old books, but -íomar is the standard now. And as Jenna says, d'éirigh muid is perfectly fine and it is what most people say out loud, so use that in the oral if it is quicker for you.

The handy thing is once you have that pattern you have every -igh verb, not just this one.

Hey! Just wondering if anyone can recommend a good website for translating words/verbs?
I struggled with the homework because some of the sentences we had to translate included verbs that weren't among the 11 irregular verbs we were given. I used google translate for some sentences but I don't think it's always accurate.

comments.body:
Hi Amy

Yes there are two, one for English Irish www.focloir.ie, and one for Irish English www.teanglann.ie. They have lots of useful resources including grammar. Just leave out the h or úru when putting in the words to search. Best of Luck. Úna
Aw thanks so much Una. I really apprecite it.

Hey Amy, great question, and Úna has you sorted with the two main ones 👍

Two extra bits on those sites that people often miss:

- On teanglann.ie, when you look up a verb there's a "Gramadach" tab that gives you the full conjugation, every tense, so you never have to guess an ending.
- Both sites have audio in three dialects, so click the speaker and say it after them. That does more for the oral than reading it off the page.

On Google Translate, you're right to be suspicious. It's fine for a single noun, it's not reliable for a verb in a tense or for anything with a preposition.

One thing that will save you time: rather than translating each sentence from scratch, keep a small list of the verbs that keep coming up in your own material, with the past, present and future beside them. Ten or twelve verbs you actually control will carry you further in the oral than fifty you looked up once.

If a sentence in the homework won't come right, fire it over to me here and I'll take a look.

Fáilte romhat! 👋

To kick things off, I’d love you to introduce yourself in the comments and answer one simple question:

Why do you want to become a teacher?

It could be something you’ve wanted for years, a teacher who inspired you, or simply the chance to make a difference in children’s lives.

I’ll go first so nobody else has to be the one to break the ice!

Is mise Éamon agus is as Contae Uíbh Fhailí mé. (I’m Éamon and I’m from County Offaly.) This is my 7th year teaching this course, agus tá an-áthas orm a bheith ar ais arís i mbliana. (I’m delighted to be back again this year.)

My aim has always been to help people see Irish for what it really is: teanga bheo (a living language) that can be learned, spoken and enjoyed by anyone who is willing to put in the effort.

Every year, this is my absolute favourite course to teach. Knowing the impact a great teacher can have, I feel incredibly lucky to play a small part in helping so many brilliant people become teachers.

Is breá liom a bheith ag múineadh. (I love teaching.) Helping other people through teaching is something I really enjoy, and, all things going well, it’s something I’ll still be doing when I’m old!

Hi all. I’m Kim, from Dublin. After teaching English in Bali, I realised that working with children was something I genuinely found rewarding. It was one of the best experiences of my life so far. I loved bringing fun energy to the classroom and watching the children develop. And I’m now hoping to pursue teaching as a long-term career here at home. I’m excited for the journey ahead☺️🇮🇪

Dia dhaoibh, My name is Ciara and I always intended to do teaching but after my L8 degree I started working and kept putting it off.. so here we are! I recently got speaking with my sons teacher, who is amazing and found out she done Hibernia at 30 so that gave me the inspiration to try now! Looking forward to the next few months.

Dia dhaoibh. Is mise Aine Maire. I'm from Galway. I'm a mum of three. My youngest is 4 and still in pre school. As the time approaches where he will be going to Primary school next year, I thought it was time to re-train. My under graduate is IT&T. 
I've always considered myself weak at Irish so I have a lot to learn. I am nervous but looking forward it.
Hi Andrea, maith thú! Loved reading this, we'll get you there together bit by bit. Looking forward to the bliain ahead 😊
Hi Laura, lovely part of the country. Táim ag tnúth (looking forward) to working with you this year and helping you become a teacher! 😊
Hi Conor, maith thú! You've the experience already, now we'll get the Gaeilge to match. Looking forward to working with you this year 😊
Hi Zac, what a lovely reason to make the jump. Ná bíodh imní ort (don't worry), everyone arrives here nervous. Looking forward to the year ahead 😊
Hi Hannah, We'll build it back up bit by bit. Fáilte romhat 😊
Hi Shania, a great why. Plenty here are starting from scratch too, so you're in good company. We'll get you there 😊
Hi Chloe, the jump from ordinary to higher is very doable, I've seen it done many times. We'll take it céim ar chéim (step by step) 😊
Hi Gary, sounds like you made the right call. The H4 is the last box to tick and we'll get you there for next summer 😊
Hi Emily, falling out of love with Irish in secondary is the most common story here. We'll get the grá back, and the speaking too 😊
Hi Laura, never too late to go after the thing you're actually passionate about. Five years of Irish is more than you think, it comes back quicker than you'd expect 😊
Hi Chloe, great first step and you've the experience behind you already. Fáilte romhat, looking forward to the year 😊
Hi Páidí, tá Gaeilge bhreá agat (you've lovely Irish)! Great to see the grá there already. Céim ar chéim and we'll get you there 😊
Hi Jenna, that was some leap to make and it clearly paid off. We'll get that grá for the Gaeilge back this year 😊
Hi Seán, great to have the inspiration close to home. If your sister did it, so can you. Looking forward to working with you 😊
Hi Abbie, biting the bullet is the hardest part and you've done it. Nerves are normal, we'll take it bit by bit 😊
Hi Amy, eight years is a lot of experience to bring with you. The confidence to speak will come, that's exactly what this year is for 😊
Hi Shauna, being a chapter in their story is a beautiful way to put it. Looking forward to helping you get there 😊
Hi Seán-Glenn, Gaeilge mhaith agat cheana féin (good Irish already)! Holding a conversation as Gaeilge is well within reach this year 😊
Hi Leah, placement has a way of making the decision for you! The confidence is what we'll build this year, bit by bit 😊
Hi Laura, lovely reason and great grounding for the classroom. Táim ag tnúth (looking forward) to the year ahead with you 😊
Hi Emily, fair play for making the jump. Nervous is grand, we'll get you through the Leaving Cert together 😊
Hi Seán, taithí iontach ansin! Great to have you home and on board 😊
Hi Jennifer, you did honours before so the foundation is already there. Excited, nervous is a common mix, we'll get you there together 😊
Hi Gemma, six years in Early Years is a great grounding. The Irish is the last piece and we'll sort that this year 😊
Hi Mary, chasing it for your own children as much as yourself, love that. We'll get the Irish grade sorted together 😊
Hi Michelle, nine years in a Gaelscoil means you've far more Irish in you than you think! 😊
Hi Aela, the confidence part is often the biggest hurdle of the lot. Focus on the H4 and we'll take it céim ar chéim (step by step) 😊
Hi Áine, the dialect switch catches a lot of people out. Very fixable, and the H4 for Hibernia is well within reach 😊
Hi Kristi, five years as an SNA is great preparation. Fáilte romhat, looking forward to working with you this year 😊
Hi Clodagh, no better time than now. The Irish is the last hurdle and we'll clear it together 😊
Hi Kacey, nothing impossible about it, plenty here have done exactly this. Let's make this the go that counts 😊
Hi Sarah, what a year you've had already! Coming back to education on your own terms is a completely different thing. Looking forward to the year ahead 😊
Hi Rebecca, still remembering your own primary teachers is a lovely reason to make the move. Looking forward to working with you 😊
Hi Maeve, teaching in the blood then! Clearing the Irish hurdle is exactly what this year is for 😊
Hi Jack, four years in Mary I is a great start. Re-immersing is the right way to think about it, we'll take it bit by bit 😊
Hi Mary, teaching abroad has a way of showing you what you actually want. You'll remember more Irish than you expect 😊
Hi Kim, bringing that fun energy into an Irish classroom here is exactly what we need. Looking forward to the year ahead 😊
Hi Ciara, great inspiration to have. Never too late, and here we are! Looking forward to working with you this year 😊
Hi Áine Máire, fáilte ar an gcúrsa. Nerves is normal, we'll build it up bit by bit 😊

Dia dhaoibh, Is mise Holly de Brún. I'm from Cavan.
I just finished my undergraduate degree and I am beginning a masters but I've never been able to shake the desire to teach.
I am quite dyslexic and only began learning Irish at age 8, so I believed Irish wasn't for me when I was in school. But I have huge respect for the language and I would love to become fluent. Further, I hope to do a PME next year. Most importantly, I had an excellent primary school teacher who I think was instrumental in shaping my academic potential, and life outside of education. I would love the opportunity to pass that forward.

Hi,
Sorry I'm late to the party, I only joined last night.  I'm Sarah, 34 year old, mammy of 2.  I work in a primary school in Dublin as an SNA the past 11 years.  I always wanted to be a primary school teacher but unfortunately I did my Junior Cert and Leaving Cert Irish at ordinary level.  I struggled a lot with Irish in school and therefore never believed I could do it. I completed a level 8 degree in Education and training at DCU in 2020.  My plan was to then do my Irish and then Hibernia but COVID happened and life got in the way. So here I am finally!

Hi! Is mise Patrice agus táim in mo chónaí i Léim an Bhradáin, Contae Cill Dara. 

I’ve wanted to pursue Primary School Teaching for a long time. Almost 20 years ago I resat the Irish LC and missed it by a couple of marks. Then life takes over… so here I am again almost 20 years later, trying one more time! I’m currently working as an SNA in Dublin, I LOVE it! Love being part of the school environment. I’m excited to be making this step again. Thanks!

Dia daoibh! I'm Sarah, I'm living in Cavan but went through school in the UK so never sat a leaving cert, and up until a couple of years ago the extent of my Irish was tae, siúcra agus bainne. It's not convinced it's a great deal better now to be honest but I've been fairly ok with language learning in the past and I'm determined to have a good go! I've wanted to study to become a primary teacher for over 10 years now but with work and my little lad, I have just never got around to it. Hoping to take the plunge now, depending on how this goes. All the very best to you all :)

threads.title: Dia dhaoibh
threads.body:
Hi gach duine, 

Béibhinn is ainm dom, agus is as Connamara mé, i gContae na Gaillimhe (My name is Béibhinn, and I am from Connamara in county Galway). I will be helping out throughout the year as you are learning Irish, answering your questions and helping with the obair bhaile. 

D'fhás mé suas ag labhairt Gaeilge agus chuaigh mé chuig scoil lán-Gaeilge (I grew up speaking Irish and attended an all Irish school). I have am passionate about the Irish language and want to make sure people continue learning it in order to speak it with other Gaeilgeoirí in day to day life. 

Má tá aon cheist (if there are any questions), send them in and I will do my best to answer! 

Slán go fóill, 
Béibhinn 😊

threads.title: Dia Duit
threads.body:
Hi everyone, My name is Leona and I'm 33 years old. I have always had a passion for primary school teaching but unfortunately was not interested in studying when I was doing my leaving cert many moons ago.

I decided to do a BA in Early Childhood Care and then I travelled to Abu Dhabi where I had worked for 5 years as a primary school teacher, I then continued my travels to Australia for a few more years and then last year I returned back home to Ireland. 

I subbed in schools last year and absolutely loved it, so here I am back to the books and finally hope to finally finish my qualifications and become fully qualified. 

Best of Luck everyone :) 

Leona.

comments.body:
Leona, welcome aboard! :) You already have some experience in Abu Dhabi. This will really help you when you do the English component of your Hibernia entrance oral.

We’ll be here every step of the way and I look forward to working with you this year.
WOW ! Abu Dhabi.....so exotic.

threads.title: Obair Bhaile (Homework)
threads.body:
Dia daoibh, a chairde! 👋

I’m delighted that you joined us for our first class. Maith sibh! A huge well done on taking the first step on your journey towards becoming a primary school teacher.

Obair bhaile na seachtaine seo | This week’s homework:

* Answer the five questions for your Fáiltiú in the Homework section.
* Learn and practise your answers. Beimid ag cur na gceisteanna ar a chéile (asking each other) next week, so come prepared!
* If you’re struggling with pronunciation, use Abair.ie

I’d also recommend watching ( when you get a chance.

Finally, ná déanaigí dearmad (don't forget) ar an weekly check-in, which opens this Friday at 10am.

Go n-éirí go geal libh! 😊

threads.title: About me
threads.body:
😊
Divorced Mom of 1. Did my LC a long time ago and failed in Irish, cos I saw it as a waste of time and how were you supposed to know what the words meant when they kept changing the spelling?!? Moved to US and became a SNA over there, caught the teaching bug then went on to do a BA. It took 5 years but I got it. I had 6 months as a teacher but then we moved home to Ireland. Got me TC number and my Garda/FBI/UK Police vetting. Doing a bit of subbing but really just want to get back into the classroom.

threads.title: A little about me
threads.body: Dia Duit gach duine, I'm Ruth, mam of 4. I worked in corporate finance for 14 years but after covid decided it was time for a change. I had qualified as an SNA, did a bit of subbing and then the principle asked would I register with the teaching council and do some substitute teaching & I've been doing that ever since. My Irish is very rusty so very nervous about trying to repeat but looking forward to the challenge.

threads.title: A little bit about me
threads.body:
Fáilte romhat, I graduated from college last year as an Early Childhood Practitioner, but primary teaching has always been my dream role. After not receiving my H4 in the Irish Leaving Cert 5 years ago, I have decided to get the ball rolling for my journey to becoming a primary school teacher. So looking forward to this next chapter. 
Slán go fóill, 
Carla.
